title: How Pirates Survived Months at Sea Without Fresh Food in 1715
fullText: Ready. February 10th, 1722. Dawn, off the coast of West Africa. The most successful pirate of the Golden Age sits down to breakfast. His name is Bartholomew Roberts. 400 ships taken. 4 years untouchable. And this morning, his cook has built him the one dish every pirate on every ocean dreams about. A plate called Salmagundi. He never finishes it. Before the plate is empty, a Royal Navy warship comes out of the haze and a blast of grapeshot takes him through the throat. The most feared man on the Atlantic dies at breakfast. His last meal still warm in front of him. What was on that plate and why men killed to eat it? We'll get to. I promise it's stranger than you think. Because here is the truth about how pirates ate. They did not eat like kings. They did not eat like sailors. And some weeks they did not eat like humans. This story is rebuilt from the eyewitness chronicle of a buccaneer surgeon, the journals of William Dampia and Woods Rogers and the bone chemistry of 80 dead sailors whose skeletons still remember every meal. You will see bread that outlived the men who baked it. You will see beef so hard sailors carved it into buttons and wore their dinner on their coats. And you will meet the disease that killed more sailors than every battle, every storm, and every shipwreck combined. 2 million men. It starts with feeling tired. It ends with old wounds opening on their own. But you won't watch this from the shore. You'll live it through one 19-year-old who signed away his stomach for a share of silver. 3 months ago, he made his mark on a pirates's articles in a Nassau tavern. His name is Thomas, and Thomas is about to learn what the sea really serves for dinner. 3 months earlier, Nassau, the Bahamas, 1715. Thomas is 19. a runaway merchant sailor with ropecarred palms and exactly nothing to his name except a wooden bowl and a horn spoon. On his last ship, a legal ship, he watched the captain dine on roast chicken behind a closed door while the crew got one pound of wormy biscuit a day. Complain and you would be flogged for mutiny. Then in a Nassau tavern, a pirate quartermaster slid a piece of paper across the table. The articles, the written laws of a pirate ship, and one line stopped him cold. Every man has equal title to the fresh provisions. Equal. The captain eats what Thomas eats. The captain drinks what Thomas drinks. On the account, food is not a privilege. It is the law. Written down, sworn on a hatchet, enforced by vote. Here's the part that nobody talks about. Most men didn't turn pirate for treasure. Treasure was a lottery ticket. They turned pirate for this line. Because a starving sailor doesn't dream of gold. He dreams of dinner. So Thomas made his mark. Now do the arithmetic he's counting on. One green turtle roasted on the beach. That's a week of a London laborer's wages eaten in a single night. One good prize. And Thomas eats better than the man who owns his old ship. That's the promise. His stomach learn the ship's schedule before his feet did. But standing on the dock, watching barrels roll up the gang plank into the sloop's dark hold, Thomas doesn't know the other half of the arithmetic, the fresh food coming aboard. The bread, the plantains, the live chickens, all of it has about 10 days to live. After that, the clock starts, and the clock is the real captain of every ship on this ocean. Dawn, the sloop clears Nassau Harbor with 80 men aboard. Listen to the hold for a moment. Chickens in wooden crates. A goat complaining. Barrels shifting against their lashings. This ship doesn't smell like a pirate ship yet. It smells like a farm. Down the ladder. Look. Stalks of plantains hanging from the beams. Sacks of limes. Fresh bread from a Nassau oven. Still soft enough to press a thumb into. Thomas eats well on day one. Everyone does. That's not generosity. That's strategy. Eat the fresh food first because the ocean is already killing it. By day four, the bread grows green fur. By day six, the plantains are black. By day nine, the last chicken goes in the pot. And the goat is quietly measured with everyone's eyes. 10 days. That is the lifespan of fresh food on the open sea in 1715. There is no ice. There is no glass jar. Canning will not be invented for another 90 years. Every technology you use tonight to keep dinner alive, none of it exists. And here is what the treasure maps never tell you. Historians who studied pirate raids found something strange in the records. Pirate crews attacked coastal towns for food at least as often as for gold. Read that again. Half the time the most feared criminals on Earth were robbing for groceries. Because a pirate ship is banned from every legal port. No harbor, no market, no resupply. The sea is their supermarket now and it is closed. So on day 10, Thomas climbs down into the dark of the hold where 40 sealed barrels wait. The quartermaster cracks the first one open. Inside is the bread that will keep him alive for the next 3 months. It was baked 4 years ago. The quartermaster hands Thomas a pale, dusty square. It's called ship's biscuit. flour, water, and salt. Baked, then baked again, then baked twice more until every drop of moisture is gone. What's left isn't food. It's architecture. This biscuit will outlive Thomas. Some batches were cut with pea flour or powdered bone and came out so hard no human tooth could break them at all. Benjamin Franklin himself warned travelers in writing, "Soak it first or lose your teeth. So watch what every man does before he eats." Thomas wraps the biscuit against the table. Once, twice, hard, and things come out. Weevils, small black beetles that colonize every biscuit barrel on every ship on Earth. One passenger crossing the Atlantic wrote that the biscuits were so full of worms, sailors had to knock the insects out before every single bite. Knocking was the polite option. Here's the other one. On some ships, the crew waited for nightfall and ate in the dark on purpose, not to save candles, so they couldn't see what was still moving in the bread. But the ocean saves its crulest joke for last. The only biscuit soft enough to chew easily is the old biscuit. Months of damp sea air finally stales it into something teeth can manage. And by the time it is soft enough to bite, it is fully inhabited. Tender or empty. Pick one. The sea does not offer both. Thomas learns to dunk his square in his mug, wait and swallow without inspection. Within a fortnight, he stops noticing. That's the part that should disturb you, not the weevils. The adjustment. And yet, the biscuit is the good news. Because tonight, the cook is opening the meat barrels. And what's inside hasn't been meat for years. The cook levers open a meat barrel and the smell reaches Thomas before the site does. Inside, stacked in gray brine, is salted beef packed into this barrel when Thomas was 15. Preserved so aggressively, pound after pound of salt forced into every fiber that it is technically incapable of rotting. It is also barely capable of being food. Straight from the barrel, it's inedible. The cook soaks it in sea water for hours just to pull enough salt out to boil it. And after all that soaking, all that boiling, one naturalist who sailed with these men described the result perfectly. Meat like black oak. Sailors didn't just complain about it. They crafted with it. Across the ships of this era, men took their beef ration, let it dry hard as timber, and carved it into buttons, into belt buckles. Then they sewed dinner onto their coats and wore it. Take a second with that. The ration was so durable that the line between food and furniture disappeared. And if you think that's sailor's exaggeration, the proof is in their bones. Scientists analyzed the skeletons of 80 sailors from this century. The chemistry sealed in their bones still records the diet, salted beef, biscuit, and almost nothing else. Meal after meal, year after year, the menu is literally written in their skeletons 300 years later. So the cook does what every sea cook does. He hides it. Beef boiled to rags, thickened with crushed biscuit, that's lobg. Oats boiled to paste with molasses, that's burgoo. Dishes invented not to celebrate ingredients, but to disguise them. Thomas eats his portion in four bites and licks the bowl. But here is the thing. The meat, the biscuit, the salt, none of it is what kills sailors. The killer is in the water barrels. And it's been growing for weeks. Before we go any further, you need to understand one thing about the sea in 1715. The most dangerous thing aboard this ship isn't the enemy. It isn't the weather. It's the drinking water. Fresh water sealed in oak casks doesn't stay fresh. Within weeks, it turns green. Then it thickens. Algae blooms in the dark. A slime forms on the surface. And sailors learn to drink through clenched teeth, straining the water with their own mouths. That water breeds dissentry. And dissentry on a crowded wooden ship kills quietly and constantly. But beer doesn't rot like water. Wine doesn't rot. Rum never rots. So on every ship in this ocean, alcohol isn't the celebration. Alcohol is the plumbing. The official sailor's ration of this era was a gallon of beer a day. Not to get drunk, but because it was the only liquid guaranteed safe. Pirates ran the same system with rum mixed into every barrel of suspect water to kill the taste and calm the risk. We told the full story of the water war in another video. How sailors actually found drinking water at sea. It's on your screen now. But here is what rum meant to a pirate captain. And this one is written in Blackbeard's own journal. Rum all out. Our company somewhat sober. A damned confusion amongst us. Rogues are plotting. Then took a prize with a great deal of liquor on board. So kept the company hot. Damned hot. Then all things went well again. Read that back. The most feared pirate alive tracked his crew's loyalty in gallons. A sober pirate ship wasn't a disciplined ship. It was a mutiny with a countdown. Thomas drinks his ration like everyone else. Half a pint twice a day. But rum has one floor. It fills the cup and does nothing for the plate. And somewhere past the 60-day mark, the plates start coming up empty. Day 40, the barrels are half empty, and the lookout isn't watching for sails anymore. He's watching for turtles. In these waters swims the single most valuable animal in the pirate world, the green sea turtle. 200 lb of fresh meat. One explorer who sailed with these crews, William Dampia, devoted five full pages of his journal to turtles and swore the meat was sweeter than the finest chicken in England. But the real genius isn't the catch. It's what happens after. The crew doesn't kill them, they flip them. A sea turtle on its back is helpless and stays alive for weeks. So pirate crews lined their decks with upturned turtles, splashed them with seaater each morning, and kept them breathing until the day the cook needed one. Stop and look at what they built. No ice exists. No refrigeration exists. So sailors invented a refrigerator made of living animals. Fresh meat on demand, self- storing in the tropics a century and a half before the ice box. This wasn't a trick. It was an industry. In 1684, in Jamaica alone, 2,000 people ate turtle every day, supplied by fleets of turtle hunting sloops. Turtle wasn't exotic. Turtle was the Caribbean's beef. And the sea gives smaller gifts, too. Flying fish that crash onto the deck at night, ready for the pan. Sharks, seabirds. Dampia ate a flamingo once and reviewed it favorably, like a food critic at the edge of the world. That night, Thomas has the watch. The deck is quiet. Beside him in the dark, a row of turtles breathe slowly in and out. The ship smells of fresh meat and salt. For the first time in 6 weeks, his stomach is silent. He almost feels lucky. He shouldn't because two days from now, the wind stops and the arithmetic begins. Day 62. Be calmed. No wind for 9 days. No prize for 5 weeks. The goat went 2 weeks ago. Now the quartermaster does the arithmetic out loud. And one explorer of this era recorded the exact numbers from his own bearmed ship. 60 days of provisions left at half a pint of dried corn per man per day. Half a pint. About the size of your coffee cup. That's the whole day. And even that isn't safe because the ship carries hundreds of passengers who never signed the articles. Rats. They find the grain. They always find the grain, so the crew makes the oldest trade at sea. The rats eat the corn, so the men eat the rats. Fried ship's rat becomes a meal men cue for. Then the tallow candles go into the pot. And when the candles are gone, the men look down at their own belts and satchels. This is not legend. A surgeon who marched with starving buccaneers wrote down the actual recipe. Slice the leather into strips. Soak it. Beat it between two stones to tenderize. Scrape off the hair. Roast. He recorded cooking instructions for luggage. But hunger isn't what breaks a crew. What breaks a crew arrives silently in the blood. Scurvy. It starts as exhaustion so total that officers mistook it for laziness and flogged dying men for it. Then Thomas's gums turn spongy and black and begin to swallow his loosening teeth. His breath smells of rot. Then the true horror. Without fresh food, the body stops making the glue that holds it together. Scars dissolve. Wounds healed years ago silently reopen. Bones broken in childhood re-break. Men's joints creek out loud when they walk. This disease killed more sailors than every battle, storm, and shipwreck of the age. Combined, 2 million. And the cure, the entire cure, is one lime. There is one meal left that can save this crew. And it's flying a Spanish flag. Day 71. A sail on the horizon, Spanish, heavy in the water. Heavy means cargo. The chase takes four hours. The fight takes 10 minutes. And when Thomas drops into the prizes hold, he doesn't look for silver. He looks for food, and finds a floating market. Wheels of cheese, casks of madiraa wine, sugar, live pigs, crates of limes. The cure for what is already loosening his teeth, stacked to the ceiling by men who never knew what they were carrying. Tonight, nobody sleeps. Tonight, the cook builds the dish. The one from the beginning of this story. The one Bartholomew Roberts was eating the morning he died. Salmagundi. There is no recipe. That's the point. Salmaagundi is everything at once. Roasted turtle and salt pork and pigeon chopped and marinated in wine. Pickled herring, hardboiled eggs, mangoes, palm hearts, olives, anchovies. All of it heaped in one mountain, drowned in oil and vinegar, and hammered with garlic, mustard seed, and pepper. Every flavor the ocean denied them for months detonated on a single plate. It was the whole voyage's hunger answered in one dish. Blackbeard served it to the governor of Virginia like a trophy. And now you understand why the most successful pirate alive wouldn't leave his plate. Even with a warship closing in, some of that table is still on yours. The rum they drank survives in every cocktail bar on Earth. The ship's biscuit lives on as the cracker. And turtle, pirate survival food, somehow became a delicacy so prized that emperors and presidents served turtle soup for another two centuries. Thomas eats until it hurts, then eats more. Around him, 80 men who were chewing leather last week are laughing with grease on their chins. Tomorrow, the arithmetic starts again. Every feast at sea is borrowed, but tomorrow there's also a coastline on the horizon, and Thomas has been counting one number all voyage long. Day 89. Nassau Harbor opens ahead like a door. Thomas steps onto the dock with his share in his pocket. Enough silver to make his old captain look away. Enough to buy anything in port. And here's the number he's been counting since day 10. Not pieces of ate, not prizes taken. 89 days since he touched fresh bread. So follow him now, past the taverns, past the gambling tables, past everything a pirate is supposed to want to a bakery near the fort. Watch him put a piece of silver on the counter earned by cannon and starvation and trade it for the cheapest thing in the shop, a loaf still warm. He eats it standing in the street, eyes closed. That's the whole story of piracy that the treasure maps leave out. 3 months at sea. Bread he had to knock the insects out of. Beef hard enough to carve into buttons. A refrigerator made of living turtles. Men chewing their own belts in a dead calm. Two teeth gone loose in his jaw that will never sit tight again. Pirates didn't fight the Navy for gold. They fought the ocean for dinner. And the ocean usually won. So tonight, walk to your kitchen. Open the door of the quiet white box that hums in the corner. There is more fresh food inside it right now than Thomas saw in 3 months of open ocean. The richest pirate in Nassau could not buy what you keep next to the milk. Thomas survived his voyage. 2 million sailors didn't survive theirs. Killed not by cannon, but by the menu. If this look at the world before us changed how you see your own plate, subscribe. And the story of how these same men survived freezing nights and found water on a salt ocean is on your screen
